title: The Workforce Barbell: Why Healthcare and Life Science Talent Challenges are Getting Heavier
summary: Tonya Tatro, Global Vice President & General Manager, Healthcare & Life Sciences, ManpowerGroup shares why employers face a new talent reality as AI, automation, and evolving skill demands reshape the workforce, requiring organizations to look beyond hiring and invest in reskilling, workforce orchestration, and talent agility.
body_markdown:
For years, discussions about healthcare and life sciences talent have followed a familiar narrative: there simply are not enough skilled workers to meet demand. While that challenge remains very real, the story has become far more complicated.


When I speak with healthcare and life sciences leaders around the world, I hear concerns that extend well beyond workforce shortages alone. Organizations are simultaneously navigating AI adoption, workforce transformation, patent expirations, cost pressure, geopolitical uncertainty, changing skills requirements, and evolving care delivery models. Talent remains at the center of every one of those conversations, but the nature of the challenge is changing.


Today, many employers are facing what we call a workforce barbell. On the one end are roles experiencing restructuring, consolidation, or increased automation. On the other are highly specialized positions where demand dramatically exceeds supply. Between those extremes sits a growing number of jobs being fundamentally reshaped by technology, creating uncertainty about what skills will be needed tomorrow and how organizations can develop them fast enough.


Understanding this shift is critical because the workforce challenges facing healthcare and life sciences organizations in 2027 will require a very different playbook than they did just five years ago.


## **A Labor Market Being Pulled in Two Directions**


The healthcare and life sciences industry continues to face extraordinary talent pressure. Globally, healthcare and life sciences employers report some of the highest talent shortages of any sector, with


[74% struggling to find the skilled workers they need](https://www.manpowergroup.com/en/insights/2026-global-talent-shortage) . In fact, the World Health Organization projects a


[global shortage of 11 million health workers](https://www.who.int/health-topics/health-workforce) by 2030.


Those numbers suggest a straightforward supply-and-demand problem. However, many organizations are experiencing a much more nuanced labor market.


In life sciences, for example, patent expirations are creating significant pressure to reduce costs and improve efficiency. Nearly


[$300 billion in pharmaceutical revenue](https://www.evaluate.com/thought-leadership/portfolio-tactics-to-scale-the-300bn-patent-cliff/) is expected to lose patent protection by 2030, with the patent cliff projected to peak in 2027. As a result, some functions are shrinking while others are expanding rapidly. Organizations are becoming more selective about where they invest in talent while competing intensely for capabilities tied directly to innovation and growth.


## **This is where the barbell begins to emerge.**


On one side are roles facing consolidation, centralization, automation, or changing business models. On the other side are critical positions in areas such as AI, data science, cybersecurity, advanced therapeutics, regulatory affairs, and biomanufacturing. These are the roles organizations increasingly view as strategic differentiators. The challenge is that there are not yet enough people with these capabilities to meet growing demand.


## **The Rise of the Hybrid Workforce**


One of the most significant changes over the past five years is that many of the industry's most important jobs no longer fit traditional definitions. Healthcare organizations are deploying AI across clinical operations, workforce planning, learning and development, and talent forecasting.


Life sciences organizations are embedding AI into research and development, manufacturing, drug discovery, and clinical operations. What began as experimentation is increasingly moving into day-to-day workflows. By 2030, the World Economic Forum projects


[39% of skills](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/) workers need to perform their current roles effectively will change.


For example, a scientist may increasingly need data analytics capabilities. A manufacturing specialist may need to work alongside advanced automation systems. Clinical leaders may need a much deeper understanding of AI-assisted workflows. Workforce planners may rely on predictive analytics and talent forecasting tools that were uncommon just a few years ago.


These emerging hybrid roles combine traditional healthcare and life sciences expertise with digital, analytical, and AI-enabled capabilities. In many cases, employers in this sector are competing for skill combinations that remain relatively scarce across the labor market.


## **AI Is Reshaping Workforce Strategy**


Much of the discussion surrounding AI focuses on technology itself. I believe the more important conversation is about people.


Healthcare and life sciences organizations have historically been more cautious in adopting AI than some other industries. Over the past year, however, we've seen a meaningful shift from pilot programs toward broader implementation. Organizations are increasingly seeing practical applications that improve learning, workforce planning, operational efficiency, and research outcomes.


The implication for workforce leaders is clear. AI is no longer just a technology initiative. It is a workforce transformation initiative. Successful organizations will not simply implement AI tools. They will invest in helping their people use those tools effectively. This is where a human-first approach becomes especially important.


While technology can augment decision-making, improve productivity, accelerate research, and streamline operations, human expertise remains essential. In healthcare and life sciences, trust, judgment, patient outcomes, scientific rigor, and regulatory compliance continue to depend on people.


Organizations that balance technology adoption with workforce development will be better positioned to create long-term value than those focused exclusively on technology implementation.


## **Why Hiring Alone Won't Solve the Problem**


Historically, many workforce challenges could be addressed through recruiting. Today's environment is different. Even as organizations continue to hire aggressively for specialized talent, many leaders recognize they cannot recruit their way out of every skill shortage.


Simply put, skill demands are evolving faster than the external labor market can supply qualified candidates. This reality is driving increased interest in reskilling, upskilling, and skills-based workforce strategies.


Rather than focusing exclusively on credentials or traditional career paths, organizations are increasingly evaluating transferable capabilities and adjacent skills. Healthcare and life sciences employers are identifying opportunities to develop talent internally, redeploy existing employees, and create pathways into emerging roles.


Reskilling will become especially critical as organizations confront simultaneous pressures from AI adoption, cybersecurity threats, changing care delivery models, and manufacturing expansion.


The workforce barbell is not simply creating shortages. It is creating demand for entirely new combinations of skills. Employers that can build those skills internally may gain a significant advantage over those competing solely in increasingly crowded labor markets.


## **From Talent Acquisition to Workforce Orchestration**


Perhaps the most important shift I see among leading organizations is a move away from viewing workforce planning as primarily a hiring exercise. Instead, organizations are beginning to think more holistically about workforce orchestration.


My TAPFIN colleagues


[recently partnered with Everest Group](https://www.mpgtalentsolutions.com/en/workforce-orchestrated) to research and define workforce orchestration:


*Workforce orchestration is the enterprise capability to define work, identify the capabilities required, determine the optimal mix of human, partner, platform and digital labor, and govern execution through real-time intelligence and accountable decision-making. Like an orchestra conductor, today’s workforce planners have a lot of “instruments” at their disposal, including full-time employees, contractors, leaders, partners, AI agents, and automated processes. This perspective becomes especially valuable during periods of rapid transformation.*


Healthcare and life sciences organizations are navigating AI implementation, patent cliffs, cybersecurity concerns, supply chain shifts, and evolving patient expectations simultaneously. Workforce decisions can no longer be made independently from broader business strategy.


The organizations that succeed will be those that can align workforce investments with business priorities while maintaining the agility needed to respond to changing conditions.


In many ways, workforce orchestration may become one of the most important leadership capabilities of the next decade.


## **Looking Ahead**


The healthcare and life sciences workforce is entering a period of sustained transformation.


Talent shortages will remain a defining challenge, but leaders should recognize that the nature of those shortages is evolving. The emerging workforce barbell reflects a labor market where some roles are shrinking, others are growing rapidly, and many are being fundamentally redefined.


For employers, success will depend less on simply finding more people and more on developing the right skills, deploying talent strategically, and preparing workers for a future where human expertise and digital innovation increasingly work side by side.


The organizations that thrive will not necessarily be those with the largest workforce. They will be the ones best equipped to continuously adapt it. And in an industry built on improving and saving lives, that adaptability may become the most valuable capability of all.


To learn more, I encourage you to read our latest[Healthcare & Life Sciences World of Work Outlook](https://www.manpowergroup.com/en/insights/report/2027-healthcare-and-life-sciences-world-of-work-outlook) .
